tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.**

"Heavier" already carries the comparative ending -er, so adding "more" marks the degree twice. A two-suitcase contrast needs only one comparative marker before than. Drop "more" and keep the short -er form against last summer's suitcase.

Double -er plus more piles two markers on one degree, so this is **false** — "This suitcase is heavier than the one I packed last summer."
**B) My sister's flat is larger than mine.**

One-syllable "large" → "larger" before than. That is the standard short-adjective pattern for comparing two flats. Nothing extra is needed beyond the -er form.

Short "large" already takes -er before than, so the wording is **true** for the two-flat contrast.
**C) Of the three trails, this path is the worse.**

"Of the three trails" ranks a group of three, but "the worse" is only the comparative. Among three or more options you need the superlative. Swap to "the worst" so the grade of comparison matches the set size.

Three trails need a superlative, so the comparative grade is **false**: "Of the three trails, this path is the worst."
**D) The new bus stop is closer than the old one.**

"Close" is short, so "closer than" correctly compares the new stop with the old one. Two named places call for a comparative, not a superlative. The ending and the than-clause both fit.

Two named stops call for comparative closer, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) She sings more better than she did at the school concert.**

"Better" is already the irregular comparative of well/good, so "more better" stacks a second marker. Irregular comparatives never take an extra more. Keep only better before the than-clause about the school concert.

Irregular better already carries the degree, so more better is **false**; the **true** version is "She sings better than she did at the school concert."
tasks.solution_overview:
Suitcases, flats, trails, bus stops, and a school concert — everyday scenes asking whether each comparison is marked correctly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This opener targets double marking and the two-versus-many rule. Short adjectives usually take -er / -est; irregulars like better and worse already carry the comparative meaning, so stacking "more" on top is always wrong.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask two questions: Is the adjective already comparative or superlative? And does the sentence compare two things or rank a whole group? Mark true only when both the form and the grade of comparison fit.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
The evening train was quieter than the morning service.
This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.
It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.**

Five bakeries on the high street form a clear group, and Miller's is ranked inside that set. "The freshest" is the right -est form for one-syllable fresh. No most is required when -est already carries the superlative.

Among five bakeries, -est on fresh ranks the top, so this line is **true**.
**B) That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.**

English never forms "gooder." The irregular chain is good → better → best. Invented -er endings on irregular adjectives fail in careful and exam English. Rebuild the contrast with better than yesterday's soup.

Good never forms gooder — the irregular chain wants better, so the line is **false**: "That soup tastes better than the one from yesterday."
**C) The evening train was quieter than the morning service.**

Two-syllable "quiet" commonly takes -er in everyday English. "Quieter than the morning service" cleanly contrasts two trains. There is no need to stretch the line into more quiet here.

Quiet commonly forms quieter than for two trains, so the wording is **true**.
**D) This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.**

Multi-syllable "interesting" correctly takes more … than when the novel is set against the film. Longer adjectives almost never add -er. The more + base + than frame is exactly what this contrast wants.

Long interesting takes more … than against the film, so the pattern fits.
**E) It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.**

"Coldest" is already the superlative, so "most coldest" doubles the grade. Pair most only with the base adjective, never with an -est form. Strip most and leave the coldest winter walk.

Most + coldest stacks two superlatives, so this is **false** — "It was the coldest winter walk we have ever taken."
tasks.solution_overview:
Bakeries, soup, trains, a novel-versus-film pair, and a winter walk — check that each adjective picks the right comparative system.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You are sorting -er/-est against more/most, spotting mangled irregulars such as "gooder," and catching double superlatives like "most coldest." Longer adjectives prefer more/most; short ones usually take the ending.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the adjective, count its syllables, and ask whether the sentence ranks inside a group. If you see "most" glued to an -est form, or a homemade -er on an irregular, mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more taller than his twin brother.
Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.
Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.
The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.
My laptop runs gooder after the software update.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is more taller than his twin brother.**

"Taller" already carries -er, so "more taller" is double marking. Delete more whenever the comparative ending is already present. The twin-brother contrast then runs on a single clean comparative.

More taller doubles an -er form, so the twin contrast is **false**: "He is taller than his twin brother."
**B) Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.**

"Of all the desserts" ranks a whole set, so the grade must be superlative. "The less sweet" is only comparative and undershoots the group ranking. Less compares two; least ranks many.

Of all desserts demands the least, not less, so the comparative undershoot is **false** — "Of all the desserts, this tart is the least sweet."
**C) Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.**

Two-syllable "clear" commonly forms "clearer than" for a textbook contrast. The comparative ending is natural here and needs no repair. The explanation-versus-chapter pair sits cleanly under than.

Clearer than is the natural two-syllable comparative for the chapter contrast, so the sentence is **true**.
**D) The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.**

"Worse" is already comparative, and "worser" is nonstandard — "more worser" piles both errors. The fixed chain is bad → worse → worst with no extras. After noon the weather simply turned worse.

Worse already is comparative and worser is nonstandard, so more worser collapses — "The weekend weather turned worse after noon."
**E) My laptop runs gooder after the software update.**

"Gooder" is not English; the fixed chain stays good / better / best. Homemade -er forms on irregulars always fail. After the software update the laptop runs better.

Gooder is not English, so the invented form fails after the update: "My laptop runs better after the software update."
tasks.solution_overview:
Twins, desserts, a textbook chapter, worsening weather, and a laptop update — a dense run of beginner comparison traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set stacks double marking ("more taller," "more worser"), less versus least, and broken irregulars ("gooder"). Fix the comparison word itself before you worry about style.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First strip any stacked "more" or invented -er. Then check whether "of all" demands a superlative (least, not less). Irregulars bad/good have fixed shapes — do not reinvent them.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.
She chose the most cheap ticket available online.
Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.
This playlist is the best of the three we built.
The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.**

"Easy" → "easier" (y → i before -er) for the Monday contrast. That spelling shift is standard for consonant + y adjectives. The two-quiz contrast needs nothing beyond the -er form.

"Easy" → "easier" is the standard y → i spelling before than, so the wording is **true** for the two quizzes.
**B) She chose the most cheap ticket available online.**

One-syllable "cheap" wants the -est ending, not most + base. "The most cheap ticket" reaches for the wrong comparative system. Prefer the ending on short adjectives unless the -est form sounds awkward.

One-syllable cheap wants -est, not most + base, so the line is **false**: "She chose the cheapest ticket available online."
**C) Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.**

"Small" → "smaller" than the neighbour's is the standard comparative. No consonant doubling is required here (unlike "big" → "bigger"). The garden pairing sits cleanly under than.

Smaller than cleanly marks the neighbour-garden pair, so this line is **true**.
**D) This playlist is the best of the three we built.**

"The best of the three" correctly uses the irregular superlative inside a set of three playlists. Good → better → best fits group ranking without an extra most. Of the three cues the highest grade.

Best of the three is the irregular superlative a set of three playlists needs, so the pattern fits.
**E) The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.**

"Farther/further" is already comparative, so "more farther" doubles the mark. Irregular distance forms never take an extra more. Keep farther or further alone before from the hotel.

Farther is already comparative, so more farther doubles the mark — "The museum was farther from the hotel than we expected."
tasks.solution_overview:
A quiz, online tickets, neighbouring gardens, playlists, and a museum walk — spelling and irregular distance forms come into play.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm -er spelling (easy → easier), avoid "most" on short adjectives that want -est, and leave irregulars like best and farther alone. They do not need an extra "more."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the ending first, then the intensifier or "most." If the adjective is already comparative or irregular, strip any stacked marker before you tick true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.
Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.
She felt worse after skipping breakfast.
Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.
His second attempt was better than the first.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.**

"Spicy" → "spicier" for a clean two-item food contrast with the mild menu option. The -y → -ier change is standard and needs no more. Heat level is compared between two versions, so comparative is enough.

Spicier than correctly contrasts two curry versions with one -ier form, so the sentence is **true**.
**B) Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.**

Only two coats are in play, so the superlative the warmest overshoots. Between two items English wants a comparative, not the highest grade. Among many would unlock warmest; a pair keeps warmer.

**Trap:** Between the two + -est looks polished but is the wrong grade.

Between two coats blocks warmest; a pair wants warmer, so this is **false** — "Between the two coats, the wool one is warmer."
**C) She felt worse after skipping breakfast.**

"Worse" is the correct irregular comparative of bad/ill after skipping breakfast. No more and no worser — the form stands alone. The line simply reports feeling worse than before.

Worse stands alone as the irregular comparative after breakfast, so the wording is **true**.
**D) Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.**

Four rooms need a superlative, but the more quiet is only comparative. Groups of three or more take the highest grade. Repair to the quietest (or the most quiet) so the attic tops the set.

**Trap:** Of the four + more + adjective looks comparative-ready but the set size demands -est/most.

Four rooms need the quietest, not more quiet, so the comparative grade is **false**: "Of the four rooms, the attic is the quietest."
**E) His second attempt was better than the first.**

"Better than the first" correctly compares two attempts with the irregular comparative. Two items → better; a whole group → best. The second-versus-first frame is a pure pair.

Better than the first is exactly the irregular for a two-attempt pair, so this line is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Curry heat, two coats, skipped breakfast, four rooms, and two exam attempts — the two-versus-many rule is the headline.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on whether the cue phrase compares a pair or ranks a group. "Between the two" almost always wants a comparative; "of the four" wants a superlative. Keep irregular worse/better clean.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the quantity words (between two, of four, than the first). Match comparative to pairs and superlative to groups of three or more, then confirm irregular spelling.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.
This café is more popular than the one by the river.
My phone battery lasts longer than yours.
She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.
He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.**

"Tidy" → "tidier" after clearing the counter. Consonant + y → -ier is the expected spelling for this short adjective. The line reports a before-and-after look, not a group ranking.

"Tidy" → "tidier" uses the expected -ier spelling after the clear-up, so the pattern fits.
**B) This café is more popular than the one by the river.**

Three-syllable "popular" correctly takes more … than against the riverside café. Long adjectives almost always use more/most rather than -er/-est. The café-versus-café contrast sits cleanly in that frame.

Three-syllable popular correctly takes more … than against the riverside café, so the wording is **true**.
**C) My phone battery lasts longer than yours.**

"Longer than yours" cleanly compares battery life for two phones. Duration often rides on long / longer / longest without needing more. One -er marker is enough for the two-phone contrast.

Longer than yours is a clean -er duration contrast for two phones, so the sentence is **true**.
**D) She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.**

"The least expensive bike in the shop" correctly ranks cost among many options. Least + adjective is the standard superlative of inferiority. The shop is a set bigger than a simple pair, so least is right.

Least expensive ranks cost inside the shop set, so this line is **true**.
**E) He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.**

"Faster" already marks the comparative, so "more faster" doubles it. -er adverbs reject an extra more just as adjectives do. Keep only faster for the evening-versus-morning contrast.

**Trap:** Intensifying more + -er adverb looks emphatic but is double marking.

More faster stacks intensifier-style more on -er, so the evening run is **false**: "He runs faster in the evenings than in the mornings."
tasks.solution_overview:
A tidier kitchen, café popularity, phone batteries, bike prices, and evening runs — mostly clean models with one stacked adverb trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Most lines show healthy -ier, more + long adjective, -er for duration, and least + adjective for ranking cost. The clear fault is stacking "more" on an -er adverb such as "faster."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat the first four as reference forms. On the last, strip the extra "more" so only one comparative marker remains before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The river is deeper here than near the bridge.
Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.
Their dog is friendlier than ours.
She felt more happier after the phone call.
This is the worst film I have seen all year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The river is deeper here than near the bridge.**

"Deeper than near the bridge" correctly compares two stretches of the same river. One-syllable adjectives take -er for two-item contrasts. Here versus the bridge is a simple pair, not a group ranking.

Deeper than compares two stretches of the same river with one short -er, so the wording is **true**.
**B) Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.**

Only two recipes are named, so the simplest is the wrong grade. Of/between two demands a comparative, not a superlative. Simpler keeps the ranking inside a pair.

**Trap:** Of the two + -est is a common overshoot when the set size is only a pair.

Of the two recipes unlocks simpler, not the simplest, so the superlative overshoot is **false** — "Of the two recipes, this one is simpler."
**C) Their dog is friendlier than ours.**

"Friendly" → "friendlier" (more friendly is also acceptable). The -y → -ier pattern is natural for this personality comparison. Their dog versus ours is a clean two-item contrast.

Friendlier than is the natural -ier contrast between the dogs, so the sentence is **true**.
**D) She felt more happier after the phone call.**

"Happier" already includes the comparative, so "more happier" doubles the mark. Remember happy → happier → happiest with no stacked more. After the phone call she simply felt happier.

Happier already includes the comparative, so more happier doubles it: "She felt happier after the phone call."
**E) This is the worst film I have seen all year.**

"The worst film I have seen all year" correctly uses the irregular superlative for a broad ranking. Bad → worse → worst needs no extras. All year cues a wide set, so the highest grade fits.

Worst across a year of films is the irregular superlative the wide set wants, so this line is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
River depth, two recipes, friendly dogs, a happy phone call, and a miserable film — watch "of the two" especially.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Of the two" almost always blocks a superlative. Keep -ier spelling tidy on friendlier/happier, and leave irregular worst alone once the grade of comparison is right.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the cue says two, demand a comparative. If the cue ranks a year of films or a clear group, allow the superlative. Then check for stacked "more" on -ier forms.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.
He is the elder of the two cousins.
This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.
Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.
We walked further than planned before turning back.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.**

"Less exciting than the pilot" correctly softens a longer adjective across two episodes. Less + adjective + than is the comparative of inferiority. The second episode versus the pilot is a pair, so comparative is enough.

Less exciting than softens a long adjective across two episodes, so the inferiority frame fits.
**B) He is the elder of the two cousins.**

"The elder of the two cousins" is a traditional family comparative for people in a pair. Elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age — both patterns appear in exams. Of the two locks the grade to a two-person contrast.

**Tip:** elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age.

The elder of the two is an accepted family comparative for a cousin pair, so the wording is **true**.
**C) This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.**

Spelling and grade both fail — "bigest than" should be "bigger than." Double the g and use comparative with than: big → bigger → biggest. A than-clause wants comparative, not a mangled -est form.

Bigest than is misspelled and the wrong grade — than wants bigger: "This rucksack is bigger than I need for a day hike."
**D) Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.**

"The most relaxing" correctly ranks pottery among several hobbies. -ing adjectives of three syllables take most, not -est. Among her hobbies cues a group ranking.

Most relaxing ranks pottery among several hobbies with a long -ing adjective, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) We walked further than planned before turning back.**

"Further than planned" is a standard irregular comparative of distance or extent. Farther and further both work for physical distance in modern English. The walk versus the plan is a clean than-contrast.

Further than planned is a valid irregular distance comparative, so this line is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
TV episodes, cousins, a day-hike rucksack, hobbies, and an overlong walk — less + adjective, family elder, and the big/bigger spelling trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set adds comparative of inferiority (less + adjective), the family form elder, and the spelling trap big → bigger (not "bigest"). Read than-clauses carefully: they want a comparative, not a mangled superlative.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the preposition and ending on each line. Than + misspelled -est is an automatic false; less + long adjective + than is usually fine.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.
Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.
The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.
He is not as tall as his older sister.
The sequel was as good than the original.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.**

"As strong as the one from the market stall" correctly states matched strength: as … as marks sameness, not ranking, and both markers are present. The tea and the stall brew sit in a **true** equality frame.

As strong as keeps both equality markers between the two brews, so the wording is **true**.
**B) Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.**

After "as neat" you need a second as, not than. Than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality. Mixing the two systems is a classic exam slip.

**Trap:** as + adjective + than looks almost right but swaps the closing marker.

Equality closes with as, not than, so as neat than is **false** — "Her handwriting is as neat as her brother's."
**C) The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.**

"As peaceful as it did in spring" correctly keeps both as-markers for matched calm — dropping the second as would break the equality pattern. The park now versus spring uses a full as … as frame.

Both as-markers keep the park-versus-spring equality intact, so the pattern fits.
**D) He is not as tall as his older sister.**

"Not as tall as his older sister" is the standard negative equality pattern. In everyday meaning it is close to less tall than, but the frame stays as … as. The negative sits on the first as without changing the closing as.

**Tip:** not as … as ≈ less … than in everyday meaning, but keep the as … as frame.

Not as tall as is negative equality still inside the as … as frame, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) The sequel was as good than the original.**

"As good than" mixes equality with a comparative closer. Never write as … than; rebuild with a second as. The sequel-versus-original idea still wants sameness, not ranking.

**Trap:** as … than is a polished-looking hybrid that is always wrong.

As good than mixes systems; a second as restores equality: "The sequel was as good as the original."
tasks.solution_overview:
Tea strength, handwriting, a peaceful park, height in the family, and a film sequel — equality lives in the as … as frame.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Equality comparisons use as + adjective + as. If than sneaks in after as + adjective, the sentence is wrong — swap than for the second as. Negative equality (not as … as) is still the same frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for both as-markers. A lone as before the adjective with than after it is the classic trap; rebuild as … as before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She drives much more carefully than she did last year.
This bag is far heavier than it looks.
The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.
He speaks English better than I expected.
They arrived slightly earlier than the others.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She drives much more carefully than she did last year.**

"Much more carefully" correctly strengthens the comparative of a -ly adverb. Much / far / a lot can boost a single comparative without changing its form. Last year's driving is the than-anchor for one clean more + adverb.

Much intensifies one more + carefully form, so the year-on-year drive contrast is **true**.
**B) This bag is far heavier than it looks.**

"Far heavier" correctly intensifies a short -er comparative. Far + -er is natural and strong for surprise weight. The bag versus how it looks still uses a single comparative form.

Far heavier boosts a single -er without stacking markers, so the wording is **true**.
**C) The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.**

"A lot more harder" doubles the comparative by stacking more with -er. Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two. Keep a lot harder or much harder — never both more and -er.

**Trap:** a lot more + -er feels emphatic but is classic double marking.

A lot more harder piles more on -er, so the climb is **false**: "The climb was a lot harder than the map suggested."
**D) He speaks English better than I expected.**

"Better than I expected" correctly compares performance with the irregular comparative. The clause after than is fine, and better needs no more. Irregular better stands alone under the intensifier-free than-clause.

Better than I expected needs no stacked more, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) They arrived slightly earlier than the others.**

"Slightly earlier" correctly softens the comparative of early. Slightly / a bit / rather can modify comparatives without adding a second marker. Arrival versus the others keeps one -er form.

Slightly earlier softens one comparative of arrival, so this line is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Careful driving, a deceptively heavy bag, a hard climb, better English, and an early arrival — intensifiers meet single comparative forms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Intensifiers such as much, far, a lot, and slightly are fine before one comparative. They become wrong the moment they sit beside a second marker such as more + -er.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow the booster only if exactly one comparative remains. If you see "a lot more harder," strip either "more" or the -er ending — never keep both.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.
She is one of the smarter students in the class.
This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.
He is one of the tallest player on the team.
That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.**

"One of the most beautiful cities I have visited" hits all three slots: superlative, plural cities, and the frame. This is the model pattern for ranking within a visited set. One of the always packages with a superlative plus a plural noun.

**Tip:** one of the + superlative + plural noun.

One of the + most beautiful + plural cities hits the full superlative package, so the wording is **true**.
**B) She is one of the smarter students in the class.**

After "one of the" you need a superlative, not comparative smarter. The frame blocks ordinary -er forms even when students are plural. Smartest restores the highest grade inside the class set.

**Trap:** one of the + comparative -er looks almost grammatical but the frame demands -est/most.

One of the demands smartest, not smarter, so the comparative grade is **false** — "She is one of the smartest students in the class."
**C) This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.**

"One of the best meals" correctly pairs the irregular superlative with a plural noun. Best / worst fit the same frame as most + adjective. Home-cooked meals form the plural set behind one of the.

Best meals pairs irregular superlative with plural after one of the, so the pattern fits.
**D) He is one of the tallest player on the team.**

"One of" requires a plural noun, but "player" is singular. Always use a plural after one of, even when the superlative tallest is already right. Players restores the missing plural slot.

**Trap:** tallest looks finished, but the singular noun after one of still fails.

One of needs plural players after tallest, so the singular noun is **false**: "He is one of the tallest players on the team."
**E) That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.**

"Funnier" is comparative, but the frame wants a superlative. Comparative -er forms do not follow one of the. Funniest ranks the joke inside the show's set.

**Trap:** one of the + -er is the twin of the smarter trap — wrong grade inside the frame.

Funnier is comparative inside a frame that wants funniest, so this is **false** — "That was one of the funniest jokes in the show."
highlights: one of the most beautiful cities
tasks.solution_overview:
Cities, classmates, home-cooked meals, teammates, and jokes — the fixed frame one of the + superlative + plural noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember the package: one of the + superlative + plural noun. Ordinary comparatives and singular nouns after "one of" are the usual exam traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check three slots every time: "one of the," a true superlative (not -er), and a plural noun. Fail any slot and mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more she practised, the more confident she became.
The harder he trained, the better his times got.
More she waited, more anxious she felt.
The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.
The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The more she practised, the more confident she became.**

"The more she practised, the more confident she became" correctly links two parallel comparatives. Keep "the" before each comparative in this correlative pattern. Practice and confidence rise together under matching articles.

Both halves keep the + comparative as confidence rises with practice, so the correlative is **true**.
**B) The harder he trained, the better his times got.**

"The harder he trained, the better his times got" shows that -er and irregular comparatives both fit. The pairing is grammatical and natural. Training effort and race times move in opposite useful directions under the same frame.

Harder and better both sit cleanly under matching the-markers, so the wording is **true**.
**C) More she waited, more anxious she felt.**

Both articles are missing from the correlative comparative. Dropping "the" breaks the "the + comparative … the + comparative" pattern. Restore "the" before more in each half.

**Trap:** bare More … more … looks parallel but lacks the required articles.

Bare More … more … drops the required articles, so the line is **false**: "The more she waited, the more anxious she felt."
**D) The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.**

"The less we argued, the happier the evening felt" is a valid inferiority pair. Less / fewer can lead the first half without trouble. Fewer arguments line up with a happier evening under matching the-markers.

The less … the happier is a valid inferiority correlative for the evening, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.**

"The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be" is a classic time-and-cost pairing. Both halves keep the + comparative. Early booking links to lower prices in the fixed double-comparative frame.

Sooner and cheaper keep both correlative articles for booking and price, so this line is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Practice and confidence, training and times, waiting and anxiety, fewer arguments, early booking — correlative the … the … pairs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Correlative comparatives need "the + comparative" in both halves. Mixed shapes (harder / better, less / happier, sooner / cheaper) are fine; missing "the" is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read left and right of the comma. If either article "the" disappears before a comparative, rebuild the correlative before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.
He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.
Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.
The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.
They danced more graceful than the other couple.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.**

"More skilfully" correctly forms the comparative of a -ly adverb for how she paints. Long adverbs take more/most, not -er. Anyone else in the club is the than-anchor for manner, not a person-quality adjective.

More skilfully compares manner with a long -ly adverb, so the club contrast is **true**.
**B) He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.**

"Quicker" (or more quickly) is acceptable in modern usage for manner here. Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English when finishing a puzzle. Either form marks how fast he finished against I did.

**Tip:** Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English.

Quicker than is an accepted short-adverb comparative for finishing the puzzle, so the wording is **true**.
**C) Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.**

"More slow" uses the adjective where the verb speak needs an adverb. Adjective slow is not the same as adverb slowly. Recipe instructions need manner after speak, so the -ly form is required.

**Trap:** more + adjective after a verb of manner looks comparative but misses the adverb ending.

Speak needs more slowly, not the adjective slow, so the recipe line is **false** — "Please speak more slowly so I can follow the recipe."
**D) The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.**

"Better" correctly compares how the choir sang on two occasions. The adverb chain is well → better → best. Last night versus the rehearsal is a clean manner contrast.

Better correctly compares how the choir sang on the two nights, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) They danced more graceful than the other couple.**

Manner after danced needs more gracefully, not the adjective graceful. After danced / spoke / sang, prefer adverb forms. The other couple is the than-anchor for how they danced.

**Trap:** more + bare adjective after a dance/speak/sing verb is a near-miss manner error.

Danced wants more gracefully, not bare graceful, so this is **false**: "They danced more gracefully than the other couple."
tasks.solution_overview:
Painting, puzzles, recipe instructions, choir night, and a dance floor — separate adjective comparison from adverb comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When the word modifies a verb (speak, dance, sing), you usually need an adverb comparative — more slowly / more gracefully / better — not a bare adjective. Long -ly adverbs take more/most.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask what is being compared: a person/thing or a manner of action. Manner after a verb almost always wants an adverb form; mark false when an adjective leaks into that slot.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.
Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.
Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.
The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.
His answer was different from mine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.**

Latinate "superior" pairs with to, not than. Superior / inferior / preferable lock to to as a fixed preposition. Last winter's jacket is the comparison target under to.

**Trap:** superior than borrows ordinary comparative than but these Latinate adjectives refuse it.

Superior locks to to, not than, so the jacket contrast is **false**: "This jacket is superior to the one I bought last winter."
**B) Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.**

"Inferior to the earlier sketch" is the correct fixed comparative-like pattern. Do not rewrite these with homemade -er forms. The design-versus-sketch contrast rides on to, not than.

Inferior to uses the fixed Latinate preposition against the sketch, so the wording is **true**.
**C) Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.**

"Preferable to the dried kind" correctly states a preference between two pasta options. Preferable to ≈ better as a choice than, but the preposition stays to. Fresh versus dried stays inside that locked pattern.

Preferable to correctly states the fresh-versus-dried pasta choice, so the pattern fits.
**D) The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.**

Preferable never takes than. Swap than for to and keep the coastal-versus-inland contrast. The meaning is preference, but the grammar is the Latinate to-frame.

**Trap:** preferable than is the twin of superior than — wrong preposition on a fixed adjective.

Preferable never takes than — the coastal path wants to: "The coastal path is preferable to the inland route."
**E) His answer was different from mine.**

"Different from mine" is the standard British exam form. Treat different from as the safe choice in tested writing. His answer versus mine sits under from without needing than.

**Tip:** Treat different from as safe in exams.

Different from is the standard exam pairing for the two answers, so the sentence is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Jackets, sketches, pasta, coastal paths, and different answers — Latinate comparison words that lock to fixed prepositions.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Some comparison words never take than. Superior, inferior, and preferable lock to "to." Learn those fixed prepositions separately from ordinary -er / more patterns. Different from is the safe exam form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When you see superior/inferior/preferable, demand "to." Than after those adjectives is an automatic false; ordinary -er comparatives still use than as usual.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.
We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.
She made less mistakes on the second draft.
He drinks less coffee than he used to.
There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.**

"Fewer people" correctly uses fewer with a countable plural at the market. Fewer + countable; less + uncountable is the core split. People can be counted one by one, so fewer fits.

Fewer people matches the countable plural at the market, so the wording is **true**.
**B) We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.**

"Less time" correctly pairs with uncountable time before the ferry. Time, money, traffic, and advice usually take less. The amount of time cannot be counted as separate people-like units here.

Less time matches the uncountable mass before the ferry, so this line is **true**.
**C) She made less mistakes on the second draft.**

"Mistakes" is countable, so "less mistakes" is wrong in careful English. If you can count them, prefer fewer. The second-draft contrast still wants a quantity comparative, just the countable one.

**Trap:** less + countable plural is common in speech but fails careful/exam English.

Mistakes are countable, so less mistakes fails careful English — "She made fewer mistakes on the second draft."
**D) He drinks less coffee than he used to.**

"Less coffee" correctly treats coffee as an uncountable amount. Less + mass noun is the natural pairing for drinks measured as volume. He used to drink more; the reducing amount stays under less.

Less coffee correctly treats the drink as a mass amount, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.**

"Traffic" is uncountable, so "fewer traffic" fails. Fewer needs a plural countable noun. After nine the road has less traffic, not fewer traffic.

**Trap:** fewer + mass noun echoes the countable rule but picks the wrong noun type.

Traffic is uncountable, so fewer traffic collapses: "There is less traffic on this road after nine."
tasks.solution_overview:
Market crowds, ferry clocks, draft mistakes, coffee habits, and road traffic — less versus fewer by noun type.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less and fewer are comparative quantity words. Decide first whether the noun is countable plural or an uncountable mass, then pick fewer or less.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can count separate units (people, mistakes), prefer fewer. If you measure a mass (time, coffee, traffic), use less. That single test decides most of A–E.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.
The music grew more and more louder near the stage.
The waves became higher and higher before the storm.
She felt worse and worse during the long flight.
The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.
tactical_explanations:
**A) My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.**

"Busier and busier" correctly shows gradual increase with a repeated comparative as the festival nears. Adj-er and adj-er means steadily more. The week intensifies in one comparative system only.

Busier and busier marks the week's steady climb toward the festival, so the gradual pattern fits.
**B) The music grew more and more louder near the stage.**

"More and more louder" doubles the marking by mixing systems. Pick either louder and louder or more and more loud. Near the stage the volume rises, but only under one comparative pattern.

**Trap:** more and more + -er feels gradual but stacks two comparative systems.

More and more louder mixes systems near the stage, so this is **false** — "The music grew louder and louder near the stage."
**C) The waves became higher and higher before the storm.**

"Higher and higher" correctly intensifies a short comparative as the waves build. Repeat the -er form for gradual change. Before the storm the height climbs under a single repeated comparative.

Higher and higher is the right repeated -er pattern as the waves build, so the wording is **true**.
**D) She felt worse and worse during the long flight.**

"Worse and worse" correctly repeats the irregular comparative on the long flight. Irregulars can double the same way: better and better, worse and worse. How she felt declines under one irregular form repeated.

Worse and worse is a valid irregular gradual pair on the flight, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.**

"Increasingly" already means more and more, so "increasingly more difficult" is redundant. Do not stack increasingly with more. Toward the end the puzzle simply grew increasingly difficult — or more and more difficult.

**Trap:** increasingly more looks emphatic but restates the same booster twice.

Increasingly already means more and more, so stacking more is redundant: "The puzzle grew increasingly difficult toward the end."
tasks.solution_overview:
A busy festival week, stage volume, rising waves, a long flight, and a toughening puzzle — gradual-change patterns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Gradual change either repeats one comparative (louder and louder) or uses more and more + base adjective. Mixing systems — or adding increasingly to more — creates double marking.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pick one system and stick to it. If you see "more and more" beside an -er form, or "increasingly more," strip the redundancy before marking true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.
This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.
She is taller than any girl in her class.
This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.
He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.**

"No other beach on the island is as clean as this one" correctly sets up a unique equality comparison. No other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest. The island's beaches are excluded one by one so this beach stands alone.

**Tip:** no other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest.

No other + as … as marks this beach as uniquely clean on the island, so the wording is **true**.
**B) This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.**

"Cheaper than any other place we checked" correctly excludes the rest of the set. Any other keeps the compared hostel outside the group. Without other, the hostel could oddly sit inside the places being beaten.

**Tip:** any other keeps the compared item outside the group.

Any other keeps the hostel outside the places it beats, so this line is **true**.
**C) She is taller than any girl in her class.**

Without other/else, she remains inside "any girl in her class." Exclusion words prevent logical self-comparison. Taller than any other girl — or anyone else — keeps her outside the set she beats.

**Trap:** taller than any girl sounds absolute but compares her with a set that still includes her.

Without other she stays inside any girl, so the self-comparison is **false** — "She is taller than any other girl in her class."
**D) This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.**

Do not mix "the shortest" with "of any other." Superlative and any other usually fight each other. Choose either the shortest path or shorter than any other path to the lake.

**Trap:** the shortest of any other glues two competing exclusion systems into one broken phrase.

Shortest of any other glues competing exclusion systems, so the mixed frame is **false**: "This route is shorter than any other path to the lake."
**E) He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.**

"Better than anyone else in the family" correctly uses else to exclude him from the comparison group. Else / other prevents logical self-comparison. Family piano skill is ranked with him left safely outside the beaten set.

Anyone else correctly excludes him from the family piano set, so the sentence is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Island beaches, hostels, classroom height, lake paths, and family piano — advanced comparison hinges on exclusion words.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Other and else keep the compared person or thing outside the group. Without them, someone can be compared with a set that still includes that person — a classic logic trap. Superlative plus "any other" usually fights itself.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check whether the compared item is excluded. Add other/else when needed, and do not glue "the shortest" to "of any other" in the same breath.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.
She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.
They would rather stay in than go out tonight.
He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.
We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.**

"Prefer walking to cycling" is the standard comparative preference pattern with parallel gerunds. Prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund. Mild weather only sets the scene; the grammar lives in prefer … to ….

**Tip:** prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund.

Prefer … to … correctly contrasts walking with cycling under parallel gerunds, so the wording is **true**.
**B) She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.**

Prefer takes to, not than. Prefer … than is almost always wrong in exam English. Morning tea versus coffee still wants the locked to-frame.

**Trap:** prefers … than borrows comparative than but prefer refuses that preposition.

Prefer takes to, not than, so the morning drinks fail: "She prefers tea to coffee in the morning."
**C) They would rather stay in than go out tonight.**

"Would rather stay in than go out tonight" correctly contrasts two base-verb options. Would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive. Stay and go are parallel bare verbs under rather … than.

Would rather … than … pairs two bare infinitives for tonight's choice, so the pattern fits.
**D) He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.**

After "would rather" use the bare infinitive, not to leave. Delete to after would rather. Leaving early versus missing the last train stays under rather … than with base verbs.

**Trap:** would rather to + verb looks infinitive-careful but the structure bans to.

Would rather bans to before the verb, so to leave is **false** — "He would rather leave early than miss the last train."
**E) We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.**

"Prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway" is an accepted alternative with parallel -ing forms. Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering). Home cooking versus takeaway stays balanced under prefer … rather than ….

**Tip:** Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering).

Prefer … rather than … with parallel -ing forms is accepted for home cooking versus takeaway, so the sentence is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Walking versus cycling, tea versus coffee, stay-in versus go-out, early trains, and home cooking — preference structures as cousins of comparatives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preference patterns are prefer A to B, and would rather A than B. Watch the preposition (to, not than after prefer) and the bare infinitive after would rather (no "to").

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the structure first. Prefer wants to; would rather wants than plus a base verb. Parallel -ing forms keep prefer … rather than … tidy.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.
This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.
Her second cake was twice as large as the first.
The second half was half as long than the opening act.
Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.**

"Nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be" correctly intensifies a negative equality comparison. Nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as. The new café versus the old one's busyness still closes with as.

**Tip:** nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as.

Nowhere near as … as keeps the full scaled-equality frame for the café, so this line is **true**.
**B) This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.**

Keep the as … as frame — not nearly as steep as the guidebook claimed, not than. Intensifiers do not cancel the need for a second as. The trail versus the guidebook claim is still equality, only scaled down.

**Trap:** not nearly as … than keeps the intensifier but swaps the closing as for than.

Not nearly as still closes with as, not than, so the trail is **false** — "This trail is not nearly as steep as the guidebook claimed."
**C) Her second cake was twice as large as the first.**

"Twice as large as the first" correctly multiplies an equality comparison. Twice / three times + as + adjective + as is the fixed scale pattern. Cake size versus the first bake still needs both as-markers.

Twice as large as uses the fixed multiplier frame for the two cakes, so the wording is **true**.
**D) The second half was half as long than the opening act.**

Write "half as long as," not "half as long than." Multipliers still need as … as even when the idea is reduction. The second half versus the opening act is scaled equality, not a plain comparative.

**Trap:** half as … than is the reduction twin of as … than — wrong closer after a multiplier.

Half as long than swaps the closer; multipliers still need as … as: "The second half was half as long as the opening act."
**E) Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.**

"Slightly less humid than yesterday" correctly softens a comparative of inferiority. Less + adjective + than remains available beside as … as patterns. Today versus yesterday is a **true** comparative, so than is right here.

Slightly less humid than correctly softens today's humidity against yesterday, so the sentence is **true**.
tasks.solution_overview:
Busy cafés, steep trails, oversized cakes, show lengths, and humidity — scaled equality still needs a closing as.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Scaled equality (twice as, half as, not nearly as, nowhere near as) still needs a closing as. Than only returns when you switch to a true comparative such as less … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the line opens with twice/half/not nearly/nowhere near + as, demand a matching as later. Replace any than in that slot before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.
She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.
This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.
He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.
That was by far a better concert than the one in March.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.**

"Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit" correctly pairs a group phrase with a superlative. Of all / among all → superlative. The market set is larger than a pair, so freshest fits.

Of all + the freshest matches group ranking across the local markets, so the wording is **true**.
**B) She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.**

"By far the most organised person in our flatshare" correctly intensifies a superlative. By far / easily / much the + superlative is the usual package. The flatshare set is ranked with an intensified highest grade.

**Tip:** by far / easily / much the + superlative.

By far locks onto the most organised superlative in the flatshare, so this line is **true**.
**C) This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.**

With "much the," use a superlative — much the hardest, not much the harder. Much the pairs with -est / most, not a comparative. This month's crossword set wants the highest grade under the booster.

**Trap:** much the + comparative looks intensified but the booster demands superlative grade.

Much the pairs with hardest, not harder, so the booster grade is **false** — "This crossword is much the hardest I have tried this month."
**D) He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.**

"Easily the funniest host on the late-night shows" correctly strengthens a superlative ranking. Easily the + superlative is common in speech and exams. The late-night host field is a group, so funniest is the right grade.

Easily the funniest intensifies a **true** superlative among late-night hosts, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) That was by far a better concert than the one in March.**

"By far a better concert than the one in March" can intensify a comparative when exactly two concerts are compared. By far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives. March versus that night is a pair, so better after by far is allowed.

**Tip:** by far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives.

By far a better … than correctly intensifies a clear two-concert comparative, so the pattern fits.
tasks.solution_overview:
Local markets, organised flatmates, tough crosswords, late-night hosts, and concerts — intensifiers locked onto the right grade of comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Final polish: intensifiers like by far, easily, and much the usually lock onto superlatives. If the sentence clearly compares only two items, a comparative after by far can still work — but "much the harder" is the wrong grade.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the booster to the comparison grade. Of all / among → superlative; a clear pair after by far may keep a comparative. Reject "much the" + comparative.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE
